definitions.meaning: a funnel is the tall chimney of a ship, engine or factory
a rick is a haystack, and one that overheats starts fuming like a chimney

explanation.surface: A farmer wonders what vents the fumes from a haystack that is heating up.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the industrial chimney; the second reads the compound literally as a pile of hay giving off fumes, which damp hay does as it heats.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a tall industrial chimney and a fuming haystack fit the compound word, one as a fixed name and one taken literally.

definitions.meaning: an extra in a film or play, a walk-on with no lines, is also called a supernumerary

explanation.surface: A newspaper seller shouting about a special edition that is very good.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'extra' suggests a newsboy's cry; the first is a film extra, the second an intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A film extra is a supernumerary, shortened in theatre slang, and the same short word is an adjective for excellent.

parts.note: not a voice speaking up, but the pipes of a church instrument housed in a gallery high in the building

explanation.surface: Someone starts to speak in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipes up' looks like the phrasal verb for speaking; it is the instrument's pipes, up in a gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A church's pipe instrument is housed in a raised gallery, so its pipes are up there.

parts.note: a lobe is the soft lower end of the hearing organ, so it gives the word end
the organ whose end the lobe is gives the word ear

explanation.surface: Someone thinks an earlobe could make a person lovable.
explanation.walkthrough: A lobe is the end of an ear, and those two words in that order give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear someone is to make them liked or dear to others.

parts.note: to truckle is to submit fawningly, as a yesman does, and a truckle is also a low bed on castors; nods means dozes off, not agrees

explanation.surface: The thing on which a sycophant keeps nodding in agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nods' looks like agreeing; it means dozing, and 'truckle' is both to fawn and a low bed on castors.
explanation.definitionFit: A truckle is a low bed on castors, and truckling is the fawning a yesman does, so his bed suits him.

annotationWithheld.why: The Colonel's new (4), answer COME: no parse found that gives COME from the clue words; the reference behind 'The Colonel's new' is unclear

parts.note: a daily cleaning woman has a short title that is also a verb meaning scorch, so this lady is named after the very thing she is not for; the words are the title of Christopher Fry's play

explanation.surface: The title of Christopher Fry's verse comedy about a woman accused of witchcraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The play title makes you think of a witch spared the stake, but the lady is a cleaning woman whose name doubles as a word for scorching.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleaning woman in Britain is called a charlady, shortened to one syllable, which also means to scorch.

indicators.note: a destroyer wrecks what it attacks, so the word earth beside it is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A biblical aside: the one who wrecks the planet is no meek heir to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The meek shall inherit the earth, so someone full of hatred is no earth-inheritor; 'destroyer' tells you to rearrange EARTH.
explanation.definitionFit: The meek inherit the earth in the Beatitudes; a person full of loathing is not meek, so will not inherit it.

parts.note: a quotation from Rupert Brooke's poem The Old Vicarage, Grantchester

explanation.surface: A crafty ghost haunting the village near Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Grantchester is a village near Cambridge; Brooke's poem pictures the ghost of a church official there.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooke's poem names the ghost as a cleric in charge of a group of country parishes.

clue.text: Foul in relation to a Pole

parts.note: an uncle is a relation
N stands for the North Pole

explanation.surface: Something offensive concerning a man from Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' suggests a Polish person; it is the North Pole, giving N.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dirty or impure is foul.

definitions.meaning: called for by a page boy, a youngster sent round a hotel or club to fetch someone
waited on by a page, the young attendant of a king or queen

explanation.surface: Someone was either called by a youngster or waited on like a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A page is both a boy messenger who calls people and a young royal attendant, so being called or served by one fits both senses.

parts.note: high means up, as in up in the air
a minster is a large or important church, such as York Minster

explanation.surface: A question about which Essex church is the loftiest or most Anglo-Catholic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High church' suggests the Anglo-Catholic wing of the Church of England; split instead into 'high' and 'church' to build the name of a town on the Essex edge of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a town in Essex, now in east London, whose name is literally an elevated large church.

parts.note: to run goods is to smuggle them, as in gun-running, so smuggled means ran
sack is an old name for dry fortified white wine, the drink Falstaff loved, so wines are sacks

explanation.surface: Customs men search hiding places for bottles brought in illegally.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is the sherry-like wine of Shakespeare's day, so the plural gives the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransack a place is to search it thoroughly, turning everything over.

clue.text: Not sole, yet sole could be

definitions.meaning: not single, more than one in number
the fish name sole stays the same in the ..., so the word sole can be a ... form

explanation.surface: A riddling remark that something is not alone, though a sole might be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sole' first means only or single, then the flatfish, whose plural is also sole.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical form for more than one is the opposite of single, and the fish word sole can be such a form.

clue.text: Their teeth are set on edge

definitions.text: Their teeth are set on edge

parts.words: Their teeth are set on edge
parts.note: not something that makes teeth tingle, but toothed discs whose cogs are set round the rim

explanation.surface: People whose teeth are jarred by an unpleasant sound or taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set on edge' is the idiom for irritation; literally the cogs are set on the rim of a wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: Cogged wheels in machinery have teeth placed around their rims to mesh with each other.

clue.text: Support Stone to provide an issue

parts.note: a prop is a support, such as a pit prop
agate is a banded semi-precious stone

explanation.surface: Someone backs the Rolling Stones, or some stone, to produce a publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' reads like a magazine issue, but here it means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: To breed or reproduce is to produce offspring, and issue is an old word for children.

parts.note: members of the police force drive about in a patrol vehicle, rather than a force that drives something

explanation.surface: The motive power behind something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving force' means motivation; read 'force' as the police and 'driving' literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Officers of the police force drive around in a patrol vehicle.

clue.text: For the sake of what darling Oriental?

parts.note: a pet is a darling, a favourite person
E is short for east, so it stands for Oriental

explanation.surface: Someone asks, for goodness' sake, what darling Eastern person is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a gap-fill: the exclamation 'For ___'s sake!' takes this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday exclamation of impatience is 'For Pete's sake!', so the name fills the blank in a familiar idiom.

clue.text: Mail a lord thus and he's armoured

indicators.note: thus asks the words before it to be laid out in a new way, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dress a nobleman in chain mail and he will be protected by armour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mail' looks like the armour in the scene, but it is just letters: MAIL A LORD rearranged gives the plated animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American mammal is covered in bony plates, a natural suit of armour.

parts.note: the branching horns of a stag, the animal hunters stalk, not the branches of a stalked plant

explanation.surface: Boughs of a plant that has stalks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stalked' suggests a plant with stems; it is a deer that has been stalked, whose horns branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag's branching horns are the trophy of the stalker who hunts deer.

clue.text: Gave away secret permit to board

parts.note: to let is to permit or allow
to board a bus or train is to get on it

explanation.surface: Someone leaked a confidential permit to the board of directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board' looks like a company board, but it means climbing aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To let on is to reveal or disclose something meant to stay hidden.

indicators.note: turned tells us the name of the lake is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: Erie is one of the Great Lakes of North America

explanation.surface: A lake was drained and turned into dry land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned to' sounds like a lake becoming land; instead 'turned' sends the Great Lake's name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish name for Ireland, a country, is a land.

clue.text: What's to come is still unsure — in spite of this

definitions.text: What's to come is still unsure — in spite of this

parts.words: What's to come is still unsure — in spite of this
parts.note: a line from Feste's song in Twelfth Night; the clue thinks of a sign that foretells the future, which still leaves the future uncertain

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night that the future is uncertain, followed by a wry aside.
explanation.walkthrough: A portent is supposed to tell you what will happen, yet the future remains unsure despite it.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent or sign is supposed to foretell events, which is what the quotation says cannot be known.

annotationWithheld.why: Tipper in the river (6), answer PRIPET: the letters of 'Tipper' rearrange to the answer, but no separate word signals the anagram, so 'Tipper' would be both fodder and indicator

parts.note: low means moo, so a lowing company in stalls is a herd of cows in a byre, not rough people in the theatre's cheap seats

explanation.surface: Disreputable people sitting in the front seats of a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low company' and 'stalls' suggest a vulgar theatre audience; cows low and are kept in stalls.
explanation.definitionFit: Cows and oxen moo, which is to low, and are housed in stalls in a cowshed.

clue.text: To orate was wearing to the Romans

parts.note: to gas is to talk at length, so orate means gas

explanation.surface: Making speeches was tiring for the Romans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' looks like tiring; here it is a noun, clothing, the garment Romans wore.
explanation.definitionFit: The loose robe was the formal clothing of Roman citizens.

parts.note: not puns, but party games in which players act out words, often syllable by syllable, for others to guess

explanation.surface: A phrase that looks like a description of puns or wordplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plays upon words' looks like a definition of puns; it is acted guessing games built on words.
explanation.definitionFit: In the parlour game players act out a word or title for others to guess, so each round is a play on a word.

clue.text: Turn up jottings, find surgical thread

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning a word up means reading it from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: jottings are notes

explanation.surface: Someone digs out their notes to find a type of stitching thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn up' sounds like find; it reverses NOTES in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A seton is a thread or tape passed under the skin to keep a wound draining, used in old surgery.

definitions.meaning: a covered walkway with columns in ancient Greece
the school of Stoic philosophy, named after the painted colonnade in Athens where Zeno taught

explanation.surface: A row of pillars at an old public school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old School' suggests a traditional British school; it is the ancient Stoic philosophers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek covered portico gave its name to the Stoics, who met in one in Athens.

clue.text: That smouldering affair of Carmen's making

definitions.text: That smouldering affair of Carmen's making

parts.words: That smouldering affair of Carmen's making
parts.note: Carmen in Bizet's opera works in a tobacco factory in Seville, so what she makes is something that smoulders, not a passionate romance

explanation.surface: A steamy love affair started by the fiery heroine of Bizet's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smouldering affair' suggests Carmen's passion for Don José, but she rolls tobacco for a living, and her product literally smoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: Carmen works rolling tobacco in a Seville factory, and her product is a slim roll of tobacco that burns slowly.

clue.text: One of a godly throng heaven-bent

definitions.text: One of a godly throng heaven-bent

parts.words: One of a godly throng heaven-bent
parts.note: old slang for a clergyman or chaplain, who steers souls towards heaven, as an aviator steers a plane skyward

explanation.surface: A member of a holy crowd determined to reach paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The godly throng is the clergy; a chaplain is nicknamed a sky pilot, guiding his flock heavenward.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplain is slangily a sky pilot, one of the clergy who guides people heavenwards.

parts.note: a pretty flower, and also the past tense of rise, meaning got up

explanation.surface: Someone who has dressed up nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got up' suggests dressed up; read it as stood up, and the pretty one is a garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden bloom is a byword for prettiness, and the same word is the past tense of the verb meaning to stand up.

clue.text: Instrumental accompaniment for "A-hunting we will go"?

definitions.text: Instrumental accompaniment for "A-hunting we will go"?

parts.words: Instrumental accompaniment for "A-hunting we will go"?
parts.note: a woodwind instrument of the clarinet family whose name joins a short-legged hunting hound and the horn blown on the hunt

explanation.surface: A request for music to play along with the old hunting song.
explanation.walkthrough: The basset is a short-legged hound used to hunt hares, and a horn is blown at a hunt, so the alto clarinet's name fits the song.
explanation.definitionFit: The alto clarinet is named from a hunting hound and a horn, fitting music for a song about going hunting.
